content.title: UConn, Michigan State ready for March Madness battle
content.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — Yes, they've beaten both Duke and Kentucky in both the national championship game and Final Four.  Sure, they've slain Florida in a national title game, as well, via a Shabazz Napier buzzer-beater. But you could make a strong argument that the UConn men's basketball team has played Michigan State in more high-stakes games than any other non-conference opponent. They've met in a Final Four and an Elite Eight. They've clashed in early-season tournaments all over the world: from Portland, Ore. to the Bahamas to Germany. So it's fitting that, in a star-studded East Regional featuring Hall of Fame coaches and historic programs, UConn should meet Michigan State once again in a regional semifinals bout on Friday at Capital One Arena (9:45 p.m., CBS).  Call it the rubber match: the programs have split their eight meetings over the years. More importantly, the winner will face either Duke or St. John's in the Elite Eight on Sunday. The level of star power will be high on Friday night. Michigan State coach Tom Izzo owns one national championship and is in the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame. Dan Hurley owns two, and will surely join Izzo in Springfield someday.  The Spartans are led by Jeremy Fears Jr., a likely NBA lottery pick with a penchant for big shots (and cheap shots), along with high-flying Coen Carr, arguably the best dunker in the nation and a former UConn recruiting target. UConn, of course, boasts a trio of all-Big East selections: Tarris Reed Jr., Silas Demary Jr. and Alex Karaban, only the winningest player in program history. As usual, the stakes will be even higher. The programs' first two meetings were relatively uneventful: an 82-68 UConn win in Gampel in December 1998; an 85-68 rout by the soon-to-be-national champion Spartans in East Lansing on Feb. 5, 2000. Since then, their six meetings have all been on neutral floors. Michigan State handed Jim Calhoun and the Huskies their lone loss in a Final Four in 2009 at Detroit's Ford Field before a largely pro-Sparty crowd — much to Calhoun's eternal fury. Had Jerome Dyson not been injured, would the results have been different? We'll never know. Michigan State was among one of Kemba Walker's victims in the 2010 Maui Invitational. Two years later, in Kevin Ollie's first season as head coach, the teams opened the college basketball season in the inaugural Armed Forces Classic in Germany. The Huskies scored a 66-62 win, and afterwards surrounded Ollie during his postgame TV interview, a show of unity in a season where the Huskies were banned from postseason play. In 2014, Ollie and UConn topped the Spartans 60-54 in the Elite Eight before a rowdy crowd at Madison Square Garden. A little over a week later, the Huskies had won their fourth national title. Michigan State has won the past two meetings, at the 2017 PK Invitational in Portland and at the Battle 4 Atlantis in 2021. In October, UConn and Michigan State met in a preseason exhibition in Hartford. The Huskies won 76-69. They'll play in another exhibition next fall in Michigan. But those exhibitions don't rate among the many, high-stakes meetings between these programs. Friday night most certainly will.
